newsitem.title: USA: Direct IPO selects Digital Planet for offering.
newsitem.headline: Direct IPO selects Digital Planet for offering.

text.p: Direct IPO President said Tuesday the Internet equity offering group has chosen Digital Planet as the first established Internet firm to launch a direct share offering.
Perlmutter said the group had evaluated some 300 companies before selecting Digital Planet, which is a pioneer in developing entertainment industry Web sites.
Jeffrey Gaul, chief financial officer of the Los Angeles-based Internet company, said he expects the company to file an offering circular within 45 to 60 days to detail the terms of the offering.
Prospective investors will be able to view or download the circular of the Direct IPO Website at www.directipo.com after it is declared effective.

"We obviously believe that this is the way to go. We believe that this is a very viable alternative for us," said Gaul, who added the company expects its costs to be somewhere between that of a venture capital investment and a full-blown initial public offering.
"Certainly this is less expensive than a full-blown registration statement, but we are not at the point in our company's life for that (a full IPO)," he said.
Digital Planet expects to benefit from private investor interest among those who know it well.
"We have a high profile on the Web already, so certainly that is our advantage," said Gaul.

This is similar to the "affinity" model used by Spring Street Brewery, a New York brewer which took itself public on the Internet last year and whose founder is now raising money for a firm to complete more Web deals.
In setting up Direct IPO, the Marina del Rey, Calif.- based group formed an affiliation with Kensington Securities, a Scottsdale, Az., based registered broker dealer which is itself a NASD member.

Perlmutter has become a principal of Kensington, according to Direct IPO, which declined to provide details on the terms of the offering or the method of pricing, saying these had yet to be determined.
The companies have been in discussion with the Securities and Exchange Commission and with state regulators to prepare for the offering, they said.

"If done correctly, this is a very good vehicle to assist small firms. It gives them an option to the VC (venture capital) situation," said Gaul. "It gives them another choice. It isn't going to be for everybody."
